low.title: Exported activity NewPasswordActivity has no permission protection
low.description: Activity "edu.ksu.cs.benign.NewPasswordActivity" is reachable by any app on the device (Has an intent-filter and no explicit android:exported (implicitly exported)) and declares no permission. It handles NEWPASS. The NewPasswordActivity is exported via an intent-filter for the 'edu.ksu.cs.benign.NEWPASS' action but does not require any permissions.
low.impact: Any third-party application on the device can launch this activity. While the activity currently requires a valid encrypted token to display data, this increases the attack surface for token-based attacks.
low.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

reasons: Launching the activity provides no concrete gain as it still requires a valid encrypted token to display data.

low.title: Hardcoded secret key in strings.xml
low.description: The application contains a hardcoded string named 'secret_key' in the strings.xml resource file. While not explicitly used in the provided Java source, hardcoding potential credentials in resources is insecure.
low.impact: An attacker can extract this key from the APK, which may be used in other parts of the application or in future versions to authenticate or encrypt data.
low.recommendation: Remove hardcoded secrets from resource files and use the Android Keystore system for managing sensitive keys.

reasons: The finding does not establish how the key is used or what concrete gain is achieved by extracting it.

low.title: Sensitive password reset token and IV leaked in Logcat
low.description: The app logs the generated password reset token and its corresponding initialization vector (IV) to logcat using Log.d.
low.impact: An attacker with access to device logs (e.g., via ADB) can steal these values and use them to impersonate the user or reveal the associated email address by invoking the exported NewPasswordActivity.

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The android:debuggable attribute is set to true in the application manifest.
info.impact: An attacker with ADB access can attach a debugger to the process, inspect memory (including the random SECRET_KEY), and execute arbitrary code within the app's context.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
This is documented platform behavior for the declared targetSdkVersion rather than a defect.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The app targets SDK 27 and does not specify a unique taskAffinity for its activities, making it susceptible to task hijacking (StrandHogg) on older Android versions.
info.impact: A malicious app with the same taskAffinity can place its own activity on top of the victim's activity, potentially phishing for credentials or sensitive data.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
